A 39-year-old male with the complaints of generalized muscle spasms and seizures was admitted to our intensive care unit for TPE.
His complaints began 1 year before his admission.

After two years time of his discharge, he still had stiffness in abdominal muscles and lower back; but he had no painful spasms and he was able to live on his own; and his neurological consultancy revealed no necessity for re-treatment with TPE.

extractions.quote: The basis on which the authors made the SPSD diagnosis — i.e. what they relied on to reach the diagnosis. Many of these papers are old and do NOT use a formal/published criteria set, so do not look for or invent a named criteria. Instead: if the paper lists the specific findings that pointed to the diagnosis (e.g. clinical features such as stiffness/spasms/ hyperlordosis, positive antibodies such as anti-GAD, EMG showing continuous motor-unit activity, response to benzodiazepines), list all of them.

Anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti GAD) antibodies were detected in serum with a level >30 U mL -1 (normal: 0-1 U mL -1 ).
Electromyography (EMG) demonstrated a continuous motor unit activity of agonist and antagonist muscles at the same time.

To ameliorate sudden-onset spasms, the patient was treated with benzodiazepines, baclofen and clonazepam. These drugs did not alter the clinical status, so intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) therapy (0. 4 g/kg/day for 4 days) was initiated, but no improvement was achieved at all.
Magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography were normal.

After obtaining informed consent, we planned TPE for the patient in the ICU, and obtained blood samples for complete blood count and coagulometry, all of which were normal. We used fresh frozen plasma for TPE with a volume of 40 ml per body weight; and for anticoagulation 10 U/kg heparin infusion was used.
However, our patient had type 1 diabetes mellitus, and he was on insulin treatment.
